brief.topic: The Binary Balance Hidden in Three Piles

s01: Three piles hold three, four, and five stones. Can you leave a difficult position?
In Nim, remove any positive number from one pile. Taking the last stone wins.
Write the sizes in binary, using columns worth four, two, and one.
Count the ones in each column. An odd count gives one; an even count gives zero. This is exclusive or.
Our result is zero, one, zero. It is not balanced.
Reduce the first pile from three to one.
Every column now has an even count. The exclusive or is zero.
Any legal move changes one pile, so it breaks this balance.
From a nonzero result, balance can always be restored.
Choose a pile containing the highest unmatched bit. Flipping the result bits in that pile makes it smaller, and makes the total zero.
Repeating this leaves the other player facing zero, until you take the last stone.
Try a reply: the other player reduces four to two.
The sizes are one, two, five. Their exclusive or is six.
Reduce five to three. The columns balance again.
This strategy assumes the last stone wins. Changing that rule changes the endgame.

scenes.narration:
Three piles hold three, four, and five stones. Can you leave a difficult position? In Nim, remove any positive number from one pile. Taking the last stone wins.

Write the sizes in binary, using columns worth four, two, and one. Count the ones in each column. An odd count gives one; an even count gives zero. This is exclusive or. Our result is zero, one, zero. It is not balanced.

Reduce the first pile from three to one. Every column now has an even count. The exclusive or is zero. Any legal move changes one pile, so it breaks this balance.

From a nonzero result, balance can always be restored. Choose a pile containing the highest unmatched bit. Flipping the result bits in that pile makes it smaller, and makes the total zero. Repeating this leaves the other player facing zero, until you take the last stone.

Try a reply: the other player reduces four to two. The sizes are one, two, five. Their exclusive or is six. Reduce five to three. The columns balance again. This strategy assumes the last stone wins. Changing that rule changes the endgame.
